record.paper_title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
record.original_question: How should system-induced bias in federated learning be quantified and mitigated in realistic deployments, including through useful proxy metrics, root-cause analysis, stratification strategies, and scheduling or weighting policies?

evidence.quote: While the potential for bias in federated learning has been addressed in the literature ... a systematic study that qualiﬁes and quantiﬁes bias in realistic settings and its sources is a direction for future research. ... We want to encourage further research to study how bias can be quantiﬁed and subsequently mitigated. A useful proxy metric for bias is to study the expected rate of contribution of a device to federated learning.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a federated learning system in which a global model is trained by repeatedly selecting a subset of client devices from a population $\mathcal{D}=\{1,\dots,N\}$, having each selected device $i$ compute a local update from its private data distribution $P_i$, and aggregating the updates on a coordinating server. In realistic deployments, devices differ in hardware capability, network connectivity, battery level, availability schedule, and dataset size, so the probability $q_i$ that device $i$ successfully participates in any given training round is not uniform. Let the resulting trained model be denoted $\hat{\theta}$, and let the population-fair target be the model $\theta^\star$ that would be obtained if every device contributed equally. Define the system-induced bias as any systematic deviation between $\hat{\theta}$ and $\theta^\star$ (or between their downstream performance on subgroups of $\mathcal{D}$) that arises from heterogeneity in $\{q_i\}$ rather than from differences in $\{P_i\}$ themselves.

Develop a rigorous framework that:

(a) defines and quantifies system-induced bias in federated learning, including useful proxy metrics such as the expected rate of contribution $q_i$ of each device and its relationship to per-subgroup model performance;

(b) provides a root-cause decomposition that attributes observed bias to identifiable system factors (e.g., device class, connectivity, time zone, battery policy, dropout during training);

(c) gives stratification strategies for partitioning $\mathcal{D}$ into meaningful subgroups along which bias should be measured and audited; and

(d) designs client-selection (scheduling) and update-weighting policies $\pi$ such that the trained model $\hat{\theta}_\pi$ provably reduces system-induced bias under realistic constraints (limited per-round participation, intermittent availability, privacy, communication budget), while maintaining convergence and utility guarantees.

Establish quantitative guarantees relating the chosen proxy metrics, the scheduling/weighting policy, and the resulting bias of $\hat{\theta}_\pi$.
artifact.status_search_result: This is an open research direction. Subsequent work has studied client-sampling bias, fairness, and participation heterogeneity in federated learning (e.g., q-FFL, AFL, FedVARP, power-of-choice sampling), but a complete framework that jointly quantifies system-induced bias via proxy metrics, performs root-cause analysis, and provides scheduling/weighting policies with provable bias-mitigation guarantees in realistic deployments has not been established.
